summary: Return the maximum of every window of size k as it slides across the array.
mainInsight: Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order: smaller earlier values can never become the maximum once a larger value arrives, so they are dropped from the back; expired indices are dropped from the front. The front is always the window max.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.summary: Scan each window for its max.

approaches.name: Max-heap with lazy deletion
approaches.summary: Push (-value, index); pop stale tops outside the window.

approaches.name: Monotonic decreasing deque
approaches.summary: Pop smaller values from the back, expire from the front, read the front.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal. The variable `l` is unused; use `r >= k - 1`.

promptVariants: Why can smaller earlier elements be discarded when a larger element arrives?
Explain why the deque stays decreasing.
cards.answer: A smaller element that is also older will leave the window before the newer, larger one, so it can never be the maximum of any future window. Removing it keeps only potentially useful indices, in decreasing value order.
keyPoints: Never the max of future windows
Deque values decrease from front to back
cards.explanation: The front is the max of the current window.

promptVariants: What does the deque contain at each step, and how do you expire elements?
State the invariant after processing index r.
cards.answer: It stores indices within the current window in order of increasing index and strictly decreasing value, so deque[0] is the index of the window maximum. Indices < r - k + 1 are removed from the front.
keyPoints: Expire by index from the front
cards.explanation: Store indices (not values) so expiry is possible.

promptVariants: Time complexity of the monotonic-deque solution: ___
Sliding Window Maximum with a deque runs in ___ time.
cards.explanation: Each index is appended once and removed at most once (amortised).

promptVariants: Space used by the deque (window size k): ___
The deque holds at most ___ indices.
cards.explanation: At most k indices are in the window at once.

promptVariants: Why `nums[queue[-1]] < nums[r]` (strict) and why check `queue[0] < r - k + 1`? Is the variable `l` needed?
What do the two while loops do and in what order?
cards.answer: The first loop removes dominated (smaller) values from the back; with a strict < equal values are kept, which is harmless. The second removes the front index once it falls out of the window [r-k+1, r]. `l` is never advanced, so `r - l + 1 >= k` is just `r + 1 >= k` - use `r >= k - 1` and drop `l`.
cards.explanation: Pushing before expiring is safe because the window always contains r.
